explanation: In the tale, a theatre manager named Daly had children chalk the nonsense word on walls across Dublin. But quiz is recorded by 1782, meaning an odd person, and its origin remains unknown.

claims.text: There is no evidence that a Dublin theatre manager invented 'quiz' for a bet in 1791; the word is recorded earlier.
'Quiz' is recorded in English by 1782, meaning an odd or eccentric person.
The origin of the word 'quiz' is unknown.
In the legend, a theatre manager named Daly had the word chalked on walls across Dublin.

writerNotes: Counterintuitive: the bet story is a famous piece of quiz lore, so most players answer true; it is a myth. Self-check (CONTENT_GUIDE 9.3), all eleven codes confirmed true. Tellings disagree on the manager's first name, so the explanation gives only Daly. volatility: evergreen, a settled fact that cannot change; no time words, and nothing rests on knowledge newer than mid-2026. regional: a fact about an English word, the same for every player. style: Oxford spelling, straight single quotes, plain hyphens only, explanation of 33 words. myths: every claim screened against content/reference/myths.json; no entry matches. mystery and encore: nothing of either kind in a practice item. doubts: one writer search, on 1 November 2026: query 'word quiz etymology earliest recorded 1782 odd person Richard Daly bet legend'. Results included Wikipedia 'Quiz', Etymonline 'quiz', the OUPblog post on quiz, Museum of Hoaxes and Visual Thesaurus Word Routes. The summary stated that the word first appears in 1782, meaning an odd or eccentric person, citing Fanny Burney's diary, that the bet legend dated to 1791 is almost certainly false, and that the true origin is unknown. This was the only search I used for the batch.
